explanations.explanation: Gibeah of Benjamin is the spot. Saul, Israel's king, keeps two thousand men with him, and Jonathan, Saul's son, takes a thousand to Gibeah (1 Samuel 13:2). I think a thousand men is plenty to keep a young commander busy. Hold on to that name, because Jonathan's about to make some noise.

Ramah sounds like it could fit, friend, but the text doesn't put Jonathan there. Jonathan, Saul's son, has his thousand in Gibeah of Benjamin. Saul's two thousand are at Michmash and in the hill country of Bethel. Easy place to get turned around, so no worries.

Hebron is a real place, but it's not on this map. The text says Jonathan, Saul's son, has his thousand men in Gibeah of Benjamin. Saul keeps his own two thousand at Michmash and in the hill country of Bethel. Next time, check the verse before the oven timer goes off.

Saul blows the ram's horn and says, “Let the Hebrews hear!” He's calling his own people. The Hebrews are the people of Israel, and the horn goes out throughout the land. That's one loud announcement, and nobody has to ask what it means.
The Philistines already heard, friend. They found out about the attack on their own. Saul's horn has a different audience, because he says, “Let the Hebrews hear!” He's rounding up his own people.

The Moabites don't show up anywhere in this passage. Saul blows the ram's horn throughout the land and says, “Let the Hebrews hear!” That's a call to his own people. Moabites will have to sit this one out.

Gilgal it is. The people are summoned to join Saul there (1 Samuel 13:4). Remember that name, because Saul is going to be waiting at Gilgal for a good while. A whole lot of this chapter happens right there.
Mizpah is a real place, but it's not where the text sends the people. They're summoned to join Saul at Gilgal (1 Samuel 13:4). Gilgal is the name to keep in your pocket for the rest of this story.
Shiloh isn't in this passage, friend. The text says the people were summoned to join Saul at Gilgal. That's where everybody's headed. Pencil that one in and you're set.

Close, but the text puts the Philistines somewhere else. They went up and camped at Michmash, east of Beth-aven (1 Samuel 13:5). Saul and the people are gathering at Gilgal, which is a different spot. Same big army, different address.

False is right. The Philistines went up and camped at Michmash, east of Beth-aven (1 Samuel 13:5). Gilgal is where the people are summoned to meet Saul. So the Philistines are close enough to worry about, but they're not at Gilgal yet.

That's what they did. The men of Israel hid in caves and thickets, among the rocks, and in cellars and cisterns. The text says they saw they were in danger because their troops were hard-pressed. When you're outnumbered like that, any hole in the ground starts looking like a good idea.

Nobody charges anything here, friend. The text says the men of Israel hid in caves and thickets, among the rocks, and in cellars and cisterns. The Philistines have chariots, horsemen and troops as numerous as the sand on the seashore. Hiding is what the text says they did.

The text never says anyone surrendered. It says the men of Israel hid in caves and thickets, among the rocks, and in cellars and cisterns. Some Hebrews even crossed the Jordan into the land of Gad and Gilead. Hiding and leaving are what we're told, and that's what we stick to.

True. The text says, “Saul, however, remained at Gilgal, and all his troops were quaking in fear.” Plenty of people are hiding or leaving, but Saul stays put. That's a lot of shaking going on around one king.

The text says it plainly: “Saul, however, remained at Gilgal, and all his troops were quaking in fear.” So Saul stays, even with the fear all around him. Some Hebrews crossed the Jordan, but Saul isn't one of them. Gilgal is where he waits.

Yes, the troops begin to desert Saul. He waited seven days for the time appointed by Samuel, but Samuel did not come to Gilgal (1 Samuel 13:8). Every day the crowd gets a little thinner. I think a king watching his army walk off would feel that in his stomach.

The text doesn't say anyone asked for a new king. It says Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and the troops began to desert Saul (1 Samuel 13:8). Deserting means they were leaving, not holding a meeting. They just walked.

No marching on Michmash here, friend. That's where the Philistines are camped. The text says the troops began to desert Saul, because Samuel did not come to Gilgal (1 Samuel 13:8). They're drifting away from him, not charging anywhere.
That's the order. Saul says, “Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings.” Remember he's been at Gilgal seven days, waiting. Keep an eye on who ends up offering them.

Jonathan, Saul's son, and his thousand men don't get called here. Saul's order is, “Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings.” This is about offerings, not troops. Jonathan will be back later in the story.

explanations.answer: A runner to go find Samuel
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention a runner, friend. Saul says, “Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings.” We aren't told he sent anyone to look for Samuel. The offerings are what he asks for.

Not quite. The text says Saul said, “Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings.” Then it says, “And he offered up the burnt offering.” So Saul does the offering himself, and Samuel hasn't arrived yet.

False is right. Saul says, “Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings,” and then “he offered up the burnt offering.” He doesn't wait for Samuel to arrive. Samuel shows up just as Saul finishes (1 Samuel 13:10).

explanations.answer: Sought the favor of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's what Saul says. He tells Samuel, “Now the Philistines will descend upon me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the favor of the LORD.” Those are his words to Samuel, the prophet. Samuel's answer comes next, and it's a serious one.

Saul doesn't say that, friend. He tells Samuel, “Now the Philistines will descend upon me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the favor of the LORD.” His troops are mentioned earlier, as deserting him. This line is about the LORD.

Commanders never come up in what Saul says to Samuel. What he says is, “Now the Philistines will descend upon me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the favor of the LORD.” The LORD is the one he names. That's the part to remember.
That's the word. Samuel, the prophet, declares, “You have acted foolishly.” Samuel says it straight to Saul's face, with no wrapping on it. It's a heavy moment, so no joke from me here.
Command is it. Samuel says, “You have not kept the command that the LORD your God gave you…” The text calls it a command, and that's the word Samuel uses. Saul has run into a line he didn't keep.
Samuel never calls it brave, friend. His word is, “You have acted foolishly.” Saul may have felt like he had to do something, but Samuel doesn't give it that name. The text lets Samuel's word stand.
Samuel says the opposite, friend. He declares, “You have acted foolishly.” Wisely is the word you'd use for the other choice. Samuel doesn't use it here.

Promise is a good word, but it's not the one Samuel uses. He says, “You have not kept the command that the LORD your God gave you…” The text calls it a command. That one word makes all the difference.

True. Samuel says that if Saul had kept the command, “…the LORD would have established your kingdom over Israel for all time.” That tells us what was on the table. It's a sobering line, and Samuel doesn't soften it.

The text says it right there. Samuel tells Saul that if he had kept the command, “…the LORD would have established your kingdom over Israel for all time.” So the kingdom would have lasted. Samuel is telling him what he missed, and it's a heavy one.

explanations.answer: A man after His own heart
explanations.explanation: That's what Samuel says. “…the LORD has sought a man after His own heart and appointed him ruler over His people.” The text doesn't give a name here, so I won't either. It's a heavy moment for Saul, because Samuel says his kingdom will not endure.

explanations.answer: A man from Saul's own house
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, friend. Samuel says, “…the LORD has sought a man after His own heart and appointed him ruler over His people.” Nothing about Saul's house is mentioned. We'll leave it with what Samuel says.

Samuel is the prophet in this scene, but he doesn't say the LORD picked another one. He says, “…the LORD has sought a man after His own heart and appointed him ruler over His people.” That's the description he gives. It's about a ruler, not a prophet.

About six hundred is right. Saul numbered the troops who were with him, and it came to about six hundred men (1 Samuel 13:15). That's a long way down from the three thousand he picked at the start. It's a small crowd to bring to a big fight.

Two thousand was the size of Saul's group when he first picked his men (1 Samuel 13:2). By now, the troops have been deserting. The text says Saul counts about six hundred men with him. That's quite a drop.

A thousand is the number that was with Jonathan, Saul's son, back at the start (1 Samuel 13:2). But Saul's count here is different. The text says it's about six hundred men. The crowd has gotten a lot smaller.

Not quite, friend. The text says Saul and Jonathan are staying in Geba of Benjamin, “while the Philistines camped at Michmash.” They aren't packing up. The Philistines are staying right where they are.
False is right. Saul and Jonathan are in Geba of Benjamin, “while the Philistines camped at Michmash.” Nobody goes home. The Philistines stay put, and the raiders are about to go out.

Three is right. Raiders went out of the Philistine camp in three divisions (1 Samuel 13:17). One headed toward Ophrah, another toward Beth-horon, and the third down the border road. That's a lot of ground covered at one time.

The text has more than two. Raiders went out of the Philistine camp in three divisions. One headed toward Ophrah, another toward Beth-horon, and the third down the border road. Count them off and you'll get all three.

Four is one too many, friend. The text says the raiders went out in three divisions. They head toward Ophrah, Beth-horon, and the border road overlooking the Valley of Zeboim. That's three directions.

explanations.answer: The Philistines forbade Hebrew swords and spears
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives. The Philistines had said, “The Hebrews must not be allowed to make swords or spears.” So no blacksmith could be found in all the land of Israel. That's a pretty clever way to keep your neighbors unarmed.

explanations.answer: The blacksmiths all fled across the Jordan
explanations.explanation: Some Hebrews did cross the Jordan, but the text doesn't say blacksmiths did (1 Samuel 13:7). The reason it gives is that the Philistines had said, “The Hebrews must not be allowed to make swords or spears.” That's why there was no blacksmith to be found. The cause was the Philistines' rule.

explanations.answer: Saul had sent the blacksmiths back home
explanations.explanation: Saul did send some troops home earlier (1 Samuel 13:2), but the text never says anything about blacksmiths. It gives a different reason. The Philistines had said, “The Hebrews must not be allowed to make swords or spears.”

That's it. On the day of battle, not a sword or spear could be found in the hands of the troops with Saul and Jonathan. Only Saul and his son Jonathan had weapons. That's two weapon owners in the whole army.

The text doesn't hand weapons to Jonathan's thousand. It says not a sword or spear could be found in the hands of the troops with Saul and Jonathan. Only Saul and his son Jonathan had weapons. Everybody else went without.

explanations.answer: All six hundred of the men
explanations.explanation: That would be a nice sight, but it isn't what the text says. Not a sword or spear could be found in the hands of the troops with Saul and Jonathan. Only Saul and his son Jonathan had weapons. The six hundred came with empty hands.
